notes:
Spelling and punctuation: British (tumour, colour, fibre, grey, -ise), double quotation marks “ ” for speech, single ‘ ’ for quotes within quotes and for cited sentences; the pipeline check is case-sensitive and matches each entry as a plain substring of the translated paragraph, so every decision below was made with the exact surrounding sentences of both books in view.
1. ‘Öleceğimi ilk kez o sabah düşünmedim.’ → ‘That morning was not the first time I had thought about dying.’ Opens both novels (BY [37], SA [1360]) and recurs at BY [3443]. The negation is kept on the ‘first time’, which is what the Turkish denies; ‘thought about dying’ sets up the next paragraph (‘People think about death… Mine was not a thought.’) and SA [1361] (‘he had thought of his death before I had’). Avoided ‘thought I would die’ (idiomatic for laughing/embarrassment in English) and contractions, so the first line lands with full weight.
2. ‘Kapıyı açtım. İçeri girecek adamın adını henüz bilmiyorum.’ → ‘I opened the door. I don’t yet know the name of the man who is about to come in.’ A writer’s working note (BY [522], [3201]; SA [1363]); past ‘opened’ + present ‘don’t yet know’ reproduces the tense shift. In BY [3201] the preceding clause must use ‘opened’ as well (‘I opened the cover of the first file. I opened the door.’) to keep the açtım/açtım echo.
3. ‘Okurken hangi elinle tuttuğunu kontrol et.’ → ‘As you read, check which hand you are holding it with.’ Imperative note (SA [1323], BY [2801]). BY [2802] contrasts it with the shorter line ‘Okurken eline de bak’ → recommend ‘As you read, look at your hand too.’ so the ‘long sentence / shorter one’ contrast survives.
4. ‘seni ikinci kez öldürmüş gibi oluruz’ → ‘it would be as though we had killed you a second time’. Fragment designed to follow a conditional head clause in both places: ‘If it became a duty, the day we fell silent it would be as though we had killed you a second time.’ (BY [3170] in speech, SA [1735] recalled as ‘a woman’s words’).
5. ‘Bazen onları ben yazmıyorum gibi geliyor’ → ‘Sometimes it feels as if I’m not the one writing them’. Spoken in SA [1698], written as a note in BY [3203]; followed in both by ‘Ben sustuğumda da odalarında konuşuyorlar.’ → recommend ‘Even when I fall silent, they go on talking in their rooms.’ Contraction suits both speech and a marginal note.
6. Motto ‘İnsan hakikati öğrenmez, hatırlar’ → ‘Man does not learn the truth; he remembers it’ (motto field with the exclamation mark). Generic ‘Man’ is required because at SA [473] the Devil says it about humankind (‘we’/‘you’ would be wrong in his mouth), and the archaic generic suits an aphorism attributed to Ibn Arabi (SA [39], [361]). Semicolon instead of the Turkish comma avoids a comma splice while keeping one breath; the entry carries no final punctuation so ‘!’ (SA [40], [362], [473], [705], [1540]; BY [3382]) or a comma (SA [1714]) can be appended.
7. ‘Metale üç kez vuruluyor, sonra biri su istiyordu’ → ‘three knocks on metal, then someone asking for water’. The sound is later explained (SA [1666]–[1681]) as a tray set on the loose metal edge of a garden table, ‘tak, tak, tak’; ‘knocks’ keeps that scale, stays ominous on an old recording, and matches ‘knocked three times on the table’ in BY [989] and the SA chapter title ÜÇ VURUŞ (recommend ‘Three Knocks’). It is a lower-case noun phrase on purpose: BY [989] has it as a sentence, SA [1324] mid-sentence after ‘Sahnedeki kayıtta’, and the check is case-sensitive, so both places introduce it after a colon or a verb, e.g. BY ‘…the page where an old sound recording was described: three knocks on metal, then someone asking for water.’ and SA ‘The recording in that scene held three knocks on metal, then someone asking for water.’
8. ‘Kırılmış.’ → ‘Broken.’ SA [1326]/[1327] leaves open whether the word is said of a faulty tool or of the hurt person opposite (kırılmak = to break / to be hurt); ‘Broken.’ keeps both readings. The companion line ‘Kapak.’ (SA-only, also at BY [3452] with an empty glass) is best ‘Lid.’ — one word, as flat as the Turkish.
9. ‘siyah paket’ → ‘black parcel’: an unmarked, matt-black-paper-wrapped delivery left at a door (BY [169]); British ‘parcel’ is exact and gives the chapter title ‘2. The Black Parcel’. SA [1694]: ‘A door, a black parcel, a red string, a man with his right thumb taped.’
10. ‘kırmızı ip’ → ‘red string’: thin enough for a child’s wrist (BY [65]), a chair arm and a door handle, strong enough to tie a parcel at four corners (BY [169]); it is the ‘red string of fate’ and the Kabbalistic red string in BY [171] (Ariadne’s thread stays ‘thread’ there, since the Turkish has ‘ipi’ not ‘kırmızı ip’). The BY knot sentence ‘Düğümün iki ucu aynı uzunluktaydı’ is recommended as ‘The two ends of the knot were the same length.’
11. ‘Tümör’ → ‘Tumour’: the word on the report at BY [3439] (upper case, standing alone). Because the check is case-sensitive, the SA paragraphs must carry the capital too: SA [1349] as the quoted fragment ‘Tumour, possibly’ (“I heard the words ‘Tumour, possibly’, then other words as well…”) and SA [1658] by starting the doctor’s sentence with it (“Tumour position like yours is consistent with…”); elsewhere ordinary lower-case ‘tumour’ is fine.
12. Names: all fictional characters and Istanbul places keep their Turkish spelling and diacritics (Hıdıroğlu, Erenköy, Kadıköy, Nazım, Tarık, Duru, Nehir, Meralis, Hakikat Medeni — the pun on ‘truth’ is noted in the SA glossary but not translated). Only ‘Istanbul’ takes the English form. Turkish honorifics stay as loanwords attached to the name (Sefa Abi, Hakan Hoca, Muhibbi Amca, Vildan Hanım, Sefa Bey, Nazım Efendi), as in current British translations of Turkish fiction; one glossary line per book suffices. Scriptural and historical figures and places take their established English forms (see exonyms). The cat Duman and the nickname Küçük Saatçi are BY-bible decisions (recommend ‘Duman’ unchanged, ‘the Little Watchmaker’ translated).
13. Book titles as fixed by the brief: THE TRAVELLER (British double l) and THE WITNESS; BY subtitle ‘1453 — The Price of Awakening’ (BY [3199] ‘I named it 1453 — The Price of Awakening’). MARK ‘14.53 ↺’ stays untranslated.
